title: What Parents Want From a Classroom AI Platform: A Checklist for School Leaders
summary: A checklist for choosing a classroom AI platform from the parent's side: student data, safety alerts, teacher visibility, teacher training and consent.
body_markdown:
When a parent asks their school "Is my child's data used to train AI?", the principal can only answer as well as their AI platform allows. The same goes for "Who gets told if my child types something scary?" and "Can the teacher see what my child is doing?" Most of the answers parents want were decided when the school picked its tools.


Parents are being told to ask these questions. The[Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2026/09/07/what-parents-should-ask-about-ai-tools-their-kids-schools/) and[Stanford](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2025/09/expert-guide-tips-ai-schools-classroom) have both published lists of what to ask your child's school. In our[last post](https://flintk12.com/blog/parent-concerns-about-ai-in-school) , I ranked the ten concerns that come up most in parent surveys. This post turns them around into a checklist for school leaders choosing a platform, or checking the one they already have.


I work at Flint, which makes an AI learning platform for schools. Each section ends with how Flint answers that question, so you can hold us to the same checklist as everyone else. Where Flint doesn't do something, I say so.


## Is my child's data safe, and is it used to train AI?


**What parents want to hear:** a plain yes or no on AI training, that data isn't sold, and that there's a signed agreement protecting it.


About two-thirds of parents (65%) told the[National Parents Union](https://nationalparentsunion.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/National-Parents-Union-February-2026-Survey-Topline.pdf) in February 2026 that more needs to be done to protect students' personal data.


**What to check in a platform:**


- A signed student data privacy agreement for your state, or a willingness to sign yours.
- A written statement that student data isn't used to train AI models, and what the vendor's own AI providers do with the data they receive.
- No selling of student data and no ads shown to students.
- A public list of the other companies that handle student data (often called subprocessors).
- A clear route for a family to ask for their child's data to be deleted.


**Where Flint stands:** Flint doesn't use student data to train AI models, doesn't sell student data and doesn't show ads to students. The AI providers Flint uses, Anthropic and OpenAI, don't train their models on data sent through their business services by default. Flint's privacy policy commits to protecting student data consistent with FERPA and COPPA, the two main U.S. student privacy laws. Flint has signed student data privacy agreements with schools and districts across the country, holds the UK government-backed Cyber Essentials certification, and encrypts data in transit and at rest. Flint's[subprocessor list](https://flintk12.com/subprocessors) and[plain-language privacy policy](https://flintk12.com/privacy-policy-plain-language) are public.


## What happens if my child says something worrying to the AI?


**What parents want to hear:** that a person at school finds out, quickly.


Parents are clear about this for AI chatbots in general. In the same National Parents Union survey, 86% wanted laws requiring chatbots to show warnings before sensitive topics like violence or self-harm, and 85% wanted parents alerted if a child discusses harmful or illegal behavior.


**What to check in a platform:**


- Which kinds of messages it flags, and whether your school can add its own.
- Who gets alerted, how, and how fast.
- Whether self-harm alerts can be switched off. They shouldn't be.
- What the AI says to the student in the moment.
- That the tool is built for schoolwork, not designed to act as a friend.


**Where Flint stands:** Flint flags seven kinds of messages: harassment, hate, illegal activity, sexual content, violence, self-harm, and treating Sparky, Flint's AI tutor, as a friend or confidant about personal matters. Schools can add their own categories. School staff get an email with a link to the conversation, and the school chooses who reviews flags, such as an administrator, counselor or class teacher. Self-harm alerts are always on and are sent right away. Schools can't turn them off. In the conversation, Sparky responds with care and encourages the student to talk to a trusted adult, and schools can add their counselor's contact details so Sparky can share them.


Flint alerts the school, not parents. There are no parent accounts. The school decides whether and how to reach the family, which keeps that call with the people who know the child.


## Does the AI just give my child the answers?


**What parents want to hear:** that the AI helps their child learn and doesn't do the work for them.


**What to check in a platform:**


- What the AI does by default when a student asks it to write an essay or solve a homework problem.
- Whether teachers can change how much help it gives for each assignment.


**Where Flint stands:** By default, Sparky won't solve assigned problems or write work a student could turn in. It asks what the student has tried and helps with questions, hints and similar examples. Teachers write instructions for each activity, and Sparky follows them. A teacher can hold it back for a graded essay or let it help more directly for test review.


*A teacher's instructions for one activity, from a sample class with test accounts. Sparky may coach but not write.*


## Can the teacher see what my child is doing?


**What parents want to hear:** that an adult who knows their child can see how they use it.


**What to check in a platform:**


- Whether teachers see full conversations, or only summaries or scores.
- Whether they can see it live, during class, as well as afterward.
- Whether school leaders can see across classes.


**Where Flint stands:** Teachers can see every student session in the activities they create, while it happens and afterward, including any text a student pasted in. School administrators can see all student chats with Sparky, including chats outside assignments.


*What a teacher sees after a session: every turn of the conversation, from a sample class with test accounts.*


## Are the teachers trained to use it?


**What parents want to hear:** that teachers understand the tool well enough to use it on purpose, and to say no to it when it doesn't fit.


Most haven't had that yet. Only 18% of teachers had received any formal guidance on AI in a[Gallup survey](https://news.gallup.com/poll/710534/teachers-receive-no-formal-guidance.aspx) of 2,069 U.S. teachers this spring. 48% had only informal guidance, and 34% had none.


**What to check in a platform:**


- Whether the vendor trains teachers, and whether that training covers AI in general or only its own buttons.
- Whether you can see which teachers have finished it.


**Where Flint stands:** Flint's[AI Literacy for Teachers](https://flintk12.com/ai-literacy-for-teachers) course is free and self-paced: 18 short lessons across two levels, about two hours in total, with a shareable certificate for each level. It covers how AI works, judging its output, bias, data privacy, academic integrity, writing a classroom AI policy and talking with parents about AI. It doesn't require using Flint, and more than 8,500 teachers have joined it. School leaders can see each teacher's progress and send reminders. Our CEO Sohan Choudhury wrote a longer guide on[training a whole staff on AI](https://flintk12.com/blog/how-to-train-teachers-on-ai) .


## Is the teacher still teaching, and still talking to me?


**What parents want to hear:** that AI supports their child's teacher and doesn't replace the relationship, including the emails and conversations home.


**What to check in a platform:**


- The teacher decides what the AI does and reviews what students produce.
- Nothing in the tool grades a child or writes to a family without a teacher choosing to use it.


**Where Flint stands:** Teachers write the instructions Sparky follows, decide whether an activity is graded, and see every conversation in their activities. Flint doesn't message parents. The AI literacy course includes a lesson on communicating with parents about AI, because a well-trained teacher is the best person to explain it.


Durham Academy in North Carolina has used Flint since spring 2024. Its information technology director, Trevor Hoyt, described the parent response in our[case study](https://flintk12.com/blog/how-durham-academy-used-flint-to-embrace-ai-for-students-and-teachers) honestly: a small but growing group of parents worry that "our students, even at fifth grade, are spending too much time on their devices. That's something we're going to have to balance as a school." Most, he said, work in fields "where Generative AI is already making an impact," and support the school's direction. Both groups need the same thing from the school: a clear account of what the tool does.


## Will you tell me what my child is using, and can I say no?


**What parents want to hear:** a list of tools, told before they reach students, and a real alternative for families who opt out.


Only 37% of parents in the National Parents Union survey said their school had shared information about its AI policies this school year.


**What to check in a platform:**


- Plain-language privacy and safety material you can link from your own family page.
- A clear answer on consent for students under 13.
- Controls to limit or turn off features for certain grades.


**Where Flint stands:** Students under 13 use Flint with permission from a parent or the school. For school use, COPPA lets a school give that permission on a parent's behalf. Schools can turn off open-ended chat for specific grade levels. Flint doesn't have parent accounts, so parents see Flint through their child's work and through the school.


## The checklist


What parents ask What the platform needs Flint


Is my child's data used to train AI? A written no, covering the vendor and its AI providers Student data is never used to train AI models. Flint reaches Anthropic and OpenAI through their business services, which don't train on that data by default


Is it sold or used for ads? No selling, no ads to students Flint doesn't sell student data or show ads, and its privacy policy commits to protecting student data consistent with FERPA and COPPA


Is there an agreement protecting it? A signed state data privacy agreement Flint has signed data privacy agreements with schools and districts across the country, and publishes its privacy policy and subprocessor list


Who finds out if my child says something harmful? Alerts to named school staff; self-harm alerts always on Flint flags seven kinds of concerning messages and emails a link to the conversation to the staff the school picks, such as a counselor. Self-harm alerts go out right away and can't be turned off


Will I be told? The school decides; the platform shouldn't prevent it Alerts go to school staff, who know the child and decide whether and how to contact the family. Flint has no parent accounts


Does it give answers? Guides by default; teacher can adjust Sparky asks what the student has tried and helps with questions, hints and similar examples instead of finished work. Teachers write instructions for each activity to allow more or less help


Can the teacher see it? Full conversations, live and afterward Teachers see every conversation in their activities, live during class and afterward, including text a student pasted in. Administrators can see all student chats with Sparky


Are teachers trained? Training on AI in general, with progress tracking Flint offers a free, self-paced AI literacy course of 18 short lessons in two levels, with a certificate for each. School leaders can track each teacher's progress and send reminders


Is the teacher still in charge? Teacher sets the rules and reviews the work Teachers write the instructions Sparky follows, decide whether an activity is graded and can read every student conversation. Flint doesn't message parents


Can my child use it under 13? A clear consent process Students under 13 use Flint with permission from a parent or the school, which COPPA allows for school use. Schools can turn off open-ended chat for specific grades


Whatever platform you choose, run it through this list before a parent does. The answers you can't give yet are the ones to raise with your vendor.
